content: In individuals with sickle cell disease, the abnormal sickled shape of red blood cells leads to blockages in small blood vessels. These blockages result in episodes of severe pain, referred to as pain crises or vaso-occlusive crises. The pain can manifest in various parts of the body, including the bones and chest, and may persist for several hours or even days. Pain management during these crises typically involves both pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic approaches. The potential role of inhaled nitric oxide in alleviating pain during these crises has been debated. Its vasodilatory properties have been hypothesized to provide benefit, but no definitive evidence has been established to support this claim. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of inhaled nitric oxide in managing pain crises in individuals with sickle cell disease. The review also aimed to evaluate the relevance and validity of this treatment to inform clinical practice, particularly in the fields of hematology and palliative care, as recent literature has highlighted the importance of palliative care in managing these patients. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register. Additional searches were performed in abstract books from major hematology conferences, including those of the European Haematology Association, the American Society of Hematology, the British Society for Haematology, the Caribbean Health Research Council, and the National Sickle Cell Disease Program. The most recent search was completed on September 1, 2021, with ongoing study registries searched on November 19, 2021. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared inhaled nitric oxide with placebo for the treatment of pain crises in individuals with sickle cell disease. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data, including information on adverse events. Discrepancies were resolved by consulting a third reviewer. When data were not explicitly reported in the text, efforts were made to extract information from tables or figures, and trial authors were contacted for additional details. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE criteria. Three trials, involving a total of 188 participants, were included in the review. The participants were evenly distributed between males and females, with most being adults. One smaller trial was conducted in a pediatric setting and included children over the age of 10 years. All three trials compared inhaled nitric oxide (administered at 80 parts per million (ppm)) to placebo (nitrogen gas mixed with oxygen or room air) for a duration of four hours. One trial extended the administration of nitric oxide (at 40 ppm) for an additional four hours. This extended trial was assessed to have a low risk of bias overall, but the other two trials raised concerns due to their small sample sizes and, in one case, financial conflicts of interest. Limited data from the eight-hour trial were available for analysis, with the remaining results reported narratively. Evidence from one trial involving 150 participants suggested that inhaled nitric oxide may not significantly reduce the time to pain resolution. The median time to pain resolution was 73.0 hours (95% confidence interval (CI) 46.0 to 91.0) in the inhaled nitric oxide group, compared to 65.5 hours (95% CI 48.1 to 84.0) in the placebo group. This evidence was of low certainty. None of the trials reported on the duration of the initial pain crisis. One large trial assessed the frequency of pain crises during the follow-up period and found that inhaled nitric oxide may have little to no effect on the likelihood of returning to the emergency department (risk ratio (RR) 0.73, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.71) or being rehospitalized (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.11). This trial involved 150 participants and provided low-certainty evidence. Similarly, there appeared to be little to no difference between the treatment and placebo groups in terms of pain score reduction at any time point up to eight hours. However, the two smaller trials reported a reduction in visual analogue pain scores after four hours of inhaled nitric oxide administration. Analgesic use did not differ significantly between the inhaled nitric oxide and placebo groups in any of the three trials, although no analyzable data were provided. Two trials reported the median duration of hospitalization. In the largest trial, the placebo group had a shorter duration of hospitalization, whereas in the smaller pediatric trial, the treatment group had a shorter hospital stay. Serious adverse events were reported only in the largest trial, which included 150 participants. There was no increase in serious adverse events in the inhaled nitric oxide group compared to the placebo group during or after the intervention. Acute chest syndrome occurred in 5 out of 75 participants in each group, pyrexia was reported in 1 out of 75 participants in each group, and dysphagia and a drop in hemoglobin were each reported in 1 out of 75 participants in the inhaled nitric oxide group. This evidence was of low certainty. In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to determine the benefits or harms of using inhaled nitric oxide to treat pain crises in individuals with sickle cell disease. Larger, long-term trials are needed to provide more robust data. Future studies should measure and report patient-important outcomes, such as pain levels, time to pain resolution, and analgesic use, in a standardized manner. Additionally, the impact on healthcare utilization should be evaluated.
